A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching algorithms, theorem structure, and Appendices A–E. The text, equations, figure, and table are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithms and theoretical regret bounds with proofs. Table 1 summarizes analytical guarantees; neither the main text nor appendices report original empirical results.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical. Its main text and Appendices A–E contain no experimental, simulation, user-study, or data-analysis outcomes.

M1.justification: Section 3 corrects the estimator term in cExO's optimization objective from minus to plus, bringing its mathematical specification into agreement with Appendix E, equation (93). The TEWA-SE and Bandit-over-Bandit procedures are retained.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or conducts empirical training or evaluation. The revised treatment of Lipschitz losses concerns theoretical assumptions and proofs.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates comparison methods. Added citations and theoretical comparisons do not introduce evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: No experimental evaluation protocols, data splits, sample sizes, or measured performance metrics are reported in either version.

E4.justification: Neither version contains ablations, empirical robustness tests, error analyses, or case studies. The appendix revisions concern mathematical proofs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Probabilistic arguments within the regret proofs are theoretical guarantees.

E6.justification: Neither version reports concrete empirical performance results. Table 1 retains the same leading analytical regret rates; changes to mathematical bounds and derivations are assessed under T1.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 replaces smoothness-based bounds with an explicit Lipschitz argument for general convex losses, supporting a case already asserted in v1. Theorem 1 and Corollaries 1 and 3 omit intermediate terms. Appendix D corrects factors of two and the final conversion from estimation error to regret. The principal theorem set and leading rates remain unchanged.

C1.justification: Section 1.3 newly claims novelty for the already-present path-length-to-switching reduction, while Section 1.1 emphasizes unification across the three non-stationarity measures. The abstract and headline algorithmic optimality claims are retained.

C2.justification: v2 explains why the existing surrogate's fixed gradient bound avoids additional conditions, qualifies the strong-convexity comparison to alpha approximately at most one, and discusses possible sources of the path-length gap. It also notes potential looseness of the regret reduction and proposes second-order methods with restarts as future directions.

D1.justification: The existing tuning schedules, discretization prescriptions, and computational-complexity information are retained. No implementation, hardware, measured runtime, or code/data access information is added.

R1.justification: v2 adds five references, including second-order bandit methods, expert-learning work, and Stoltz's thesis. It expands comparisons with prior surrogate constructions and connects second-order methods to future extensions, without substantially changing the overall research positioning.

P1.justification: Localized additions and rewrites clarify assumptions, contribution framing, method explanations, limitations, and proofs. Author affiliations are updated. The overall section sequence and appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1's caption uses revised notation, Table 1's caption corrects the switching-regret label, and algorithm boxes move relative to surrounding text and theorems. The figure's structure and table's organization remain unchanged; no new figures or tables are introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 asserted Lipschitz coverage while its displayed general-convex proof used smoothness bounds; v2 explicitly develops the Lipschitz argument. Correcting cExO's objective sign and lower-bound calculations also improves mathematical consistency, while expanded discussion clarifies limitations. These are useful, localized improvements to the same central contribution and leading guarantees.
